szoveg_eredeti:
Researchers Establish Rigorous Evaluation Criteria for Artificial Intelligence in Carbon Accounting

Environmental researchers have established a comprehensive evaluation framework designed to audit and benchmark artificial intelligence systems applied to product carbon footprinting. As corporate organizations increasingly adopt large language models and machine learning pipelines to automate complex carbon accounting tasks across vast product portfolios, the scientific literature has lacked standardized criteria to judge their documentation, quality, uncertainty characterization, and reviewability. To resolve this governance gap, investigators conducted a multi-phase development effort combining international standards reviews, structured elicitation with corporate practitioners and third-party verification specialists, and iterative pilot testing on operational systems. The resulting framework organizes system assessment around transparent logic, empirical benchmarking against expert judgment or documented reference values, and explicit uncertainty characterization, establishing rigorous testing protocols for automated life cycle inventory mapping and cradle-to-gate footprint generation.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence in environmental accounting addresses severe labor constraints inherent in traditional life cycle assessment methodologies. Conventional product carbon footprinting demands extensive manual effort to translate unstructured procurement records into standardized inventory databases and to build complex supply chain models for products lacking primary supplier disclosures. While recent engineering studies have demonstrated that machine learning architectures can bridge data gaps and match material descriptions to environmental impact databases, automated pipelines introduce non-deterministic variability and potential model errors. Unlike deterministic calculation software, large language models can produce diverging outputs across repeated executions of identical inputs, complicating third-party verification. The new evaluation framework operationalizes data quality in strict accordance with the International Organization for Standardization definition of fitness for purpose, setting explicit standards to ensure automated outputs remain fully reviewable and methodologically defensible before corporate claims enter public disclosures.

Developing the evaluation criteria required a structured, three-phase research design documented across industry working sessions and technical reviews. In the first phase, investigators evaluated foundational life cycle assessment frameworks, including ISO 14040 and ISO 14044, alongside the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Product Standard and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development Partnership for Carbon Transparency framework. Concurrently, researchers gathered operational feedback through a multi-phase Product Advisory Group cohort comprising eight enterprises spanning seven economic sectors, involving more than sixty sustainability, life cycle assessment, and procurement professionals who tested candidate systems against internal corporate data and incumbent engineering studies. Independent verification firms operating across Europe and North America were consulted to define auditability prerequisites. During this elicitation process, several proposed evaluation mandates, such as requiring third-party verification as an initial prerequisite, demanding exact run-to-run output identity, and insisting on complete statistical confidence intervals for every calculated value, were systematically rejected as unworkable under current empirical conditions.

The second methodological phase segmented the carbon footprinting landscape into distinct operational use cases to avoid applying uniform evaluation standards across disparate computational challenges. Case 1 addresses automated life cycle inventory proxy mapping, where organizations seek to elevate spend-based greenhouse gas reporting to material-level granularity by matching unstructured procurement text to structured background inventory datasets. The primary technical hurdles in this mapping domain center on semantic ambiguity, taxonomy misalignment, and database coverage limitations. Case 2 examines automated cradle-to-gate modeling, which constructs synthetic bills of materials and process flow production graphs for complex products lacking direct database matches, presenting acute challenges in parameter estimation and structural process logic. A third scenario, encompassing standards-conforming modeling under rigid Product Category Rules or formal regulatory frameworks, was explicitly excluded from the current framework due to conflicting external reporting constraints.

To evaluate the framework under operational industry conditions, the authors applied the criteria to two deployed proprietary systems developed at Watershed Technology Inc.: an automated mapping system and an advanced cradle-to-gate modeling system. The automated mapping system deploys a dual-agent workflow in which a mapping agent augments raw text with technical domain context to query vector-indexed material libraries within ecoinvent version 3.11, while an independent quality reviewer agent assesses the selected dataset across material and emissions alignment rubrics without viewing the mapping agent’s reasoning steps. In benchmark evaluations comprising 1,198 test cases curated by six in-house sustainability scientists, the auto-mapper achieved an expert-accepted accuracy rate of 91.2 percent on clearly specified inputs. However, when tested on ambiguous inputs characterized by internal product numbers, unclear abbreviations, or generic labels like plastic part, expert-accepted performance dropped sharply to 59.7 percent, demonstrating that input data quality represents the single largest determinant of mapping accuracy.

The evaluation framework treats repeated-run variability not as an engineering failure to be hidden, but as an informative diagnostic tool capable of identifying input ambiguity and flagging items requiring human intervention. In repeatability experiments where the automated mapping model was executed ten times per item, unambiguous material names mapped to exact database titles with zero normalized entropy. Conversely, generic descriptions exhibited high normalized entropy, such as 0.57 for vague plastic descriptions that alternated between polyethylene and polypropylene datasets. In an empirical test of 1,193 items executed across ten repeated runs, flagging any run-to-run mapping disagreement routed 39 percent of the total dataset to human review, successfully capturing 79 percent of incorrect mappings and 91 percent of severe emissions deviations, while leaving a low 5.7 percent error rate among unflagged records. Flagging only items whose emission factors shifted by more than a factor of two captured 88 percent of severe deviations while directing just 22 percent of volume to manual auditing.

For complex cradle-to-gate supply chain modeling, the framework benchmarks end-to-end footprints against published Environmental Product Declarations while deploying component-level engineering sanity checks. The advanced modeling system constructs directed production graphs that estimate raw material composition, mass balances, and processing energy inputs, employing an independent review agent to evaluate component values against external literature reference points. When benchmarked end-to-end against 269 published Environmental Product Declarations across matching declared units, the modeling system demonstrated an overall median relative error of 33 percent, with an 80 percent error interval spanning from 6 percent to 98 percent.
